title: AI for Everyone: Understanding AI Without Code
subtitle: Understand what AI is, how it learns from examples, where it helps and where it fails, and train your own image classifier in a browser, with no code at all.
outcomes: Explain what AI, machine learning and deep learning are, and how a machine learns from examples
Train an image classifier in your browser with Teachable Machine, and test where it fails
Use a chat assistant on everyday work tasks and check what it tells you
Recognise AI's limits and risks, from made-up facts and bias to privacy and deepfakes
Read AI news and product claims critically, including what accuracy figures really mean
prerequisites: None: no coding, and no maths beyond percentages. You need a computer with an up-to-date web browser, such as Chrome or Firefox, and a webcam (or a few photos on your computer), plus a free account with a chat assistant such as Claude.
description:
AI is in your phone, your inbox and your workplace, and in the news every day. This course explains what it really is, without code or equations. You'll learn what artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning mean, how a machine learns from examples, and why a model is only as good as the data it learned from. Then you'll see it for yourself: in the first lab you train an image classifier in your browser with Teachable Machine, and later you set out to break it, finding the lighting, backgrounds and objects that fool it and fixing them with better data.

Along the way you'll put a chat assistant such as Claude to work on realistic tasks and check its answers fact by fact, learn where AI goes wrong (made-up facts, bias, overconfidence, privacy and deepfakes), and practise reading AI headlines and accuracy claims with a sceptical eye. The course ends with a decision brief on a real AI tool, the kind of clear, balanced advice a manager, a teacher or a community group can act on.

modules.title: What AI is, and how machines learn
modules.summary: Get clear on what AI, machine learning and deep learning mean and how a machine learns from examples, then train your own image classifier in the browser.

lessons.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning
objectives: Explain what artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning mean, and how they relate
Tell a system that follows hand-written rules from one that learned from data
key_points: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad field of making computer systems do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising speech, translating, spotting patterns or making decisions.
Machine learning is the part of AI in which a system learns patterns from examples, instead of following rules that a programmer wrote out by hand.
Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers; it powers most of today's image recognition, speech recognition, translation and chat assistants.
Generative AI produces new content, such as text, images, audio or code, that resembles the examples it learned from.
Today's AI is narrow: each system is built for particular tasks, and one that excels at a task can fail badly at a closely related one.
The term artificial intelligence was coined in a 1955 proposal for a workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956, so the field is decades old even though many of its tools are new.

lessons.title: How machines learn from examples
objectives: Describe the parts of a machine learning system: examples, labels, a model, training and predictions
Compare supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
key_points: In supervised learning a model learns from labelled examples, such as photos tagged cat or dog, and then predicts the label of examples it hasn't seen before.
Training adjusts the model step by step so that its predictions on the training examples get closer to the right answers.
The aim is to generalise, not to memorise: a model must work on new data, so it's tested on examples that were kept out of its training.

Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels, such as groups of customers with similar habits; reinforcement learning learns by trial and error from rewards, as game-playing systems do.
A model only knows what its examples show it: if they are few, all alike or one-sided, its predictions will be too.

walkthrough.title: A first look at Teachable Machine

steps.do: Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com and click Get Started. There's no account to make and nothing to install.
steps.see: A New Project page offering Image Project, Audio Project and Pose Project.

steps.do: Choose Image Project, then Standard image model, the one for most uses (the Embedded image model is for tiny devices called microcontrollers).
Look at the three panels from left to right. On the left are the classes, Class 1 and Class 2, each waiting for examples from your Webcam or from Upload.
steps.see: Each class asks you to Add Image Samples.

steps.do: In the middle, find the Training panel with its Train Model button, and open Advanced to see the settings it uses: Epochs, Batch Size and Learning Rate. You can leave them as they are.
On the right is Preview, where the trained model shows what it predicts for whatever you show it, with a confidence bar for each class.
steps.see: You must train a model on the left before you can preview it here.

lessons.title: Neural networks and deep learning, without the maths
objectives: Describe in plain words how a neural network turns an input into a prediction
Explain what transfer learning is and why it lets you train a model from a few examples
key_points: A neural network is built from layers of simple units; each unit combines its inputs using numbers called weights, and training adjusts those weights, often millions of them.
In an image network, early layers respond to simple patterns such as edges and patches of colour, and later layers combine them into parts and whole objects.
A classifier gives a confidence score for each class it knows and always picks one of them, even for an input that belongs to none of them.
Transfer learning reuses a network already trained on a huge dataset and retrains only its last step for your classes; Teachable Machine's image models build on a pretrained network called MobileNet.
Training a deep network from scratch takes a lot of data and computing power, which is why most people start from a pretrained model.

lab.title: Train an image classifier in your browser
lab.goal: Train a three-class image classifier in Teachable Machine, test it on examples it hasn't seen, and record honestly how well it does.
setup: A computer with an up-to-date browser such as Chrome or Firefox, and a webcam (or about 40 photos of each object on your computer)
Three everyday objects that look clearly different, such as a mug, a book and a banana
Download the template test_log.txt to record your results

steps.do: Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com, click Get Started, choose Image Project and then Standard image model.
Click the name Class 1 (or the pencil beside it) and rename it after your first object, such as Mug. Rename Class 2 the same way, then click Add a class for the third object.

For each class, click Webcam and use Hold to Record to capture 40 to 60 images of the object. Move it slowly as you record: turn it, tilt it and bring it closer and further away. To use photos instead, click Upload.
steps.see: Each class shows its count, such as 52 Image Samples.

steps.do: Click Train Model and keep the browser tab open and in front while it trains.
steps.see: The button changes to Model Trained, and the Preview panel starts showing live predictions.

steps.do: In Preview, hold up each object in turn and watch the Output bars: each shows how confident the model is that the image belongs to that class.

Now test it properly. For each object, try five situations it didn't see in training, such as a new angle, another part of the room or a different light. Record each one in test_log.txt: what you showed it, what it predicted, its confidence and whether it was right.
Count how many tests it got right, and write it as Right: 12 out of 15 (with your numbers).
Open Advanced, then Under the hood, and click Calculate accuracy per class and Calculate confusion matrix. Record what they show.
steps.see: Teachable Machine works these out on the test samples: the 15% of your samples it kept out of training.

steps.do: Save your project for module 3's lab: open the menu at the top left and choose Save project to Drive, or Download project as file.

checks.text: Three named classes are recorded, each with its number of samples (at least 30 each).
At least ten tests on new examples are recorded, each with what was shown, the prediction and its confidence.
The number of right answers is counted out of the number of tests.
The accuracy per class from Under the hood is reported.
The biggest surprise or mistake is described, with a sensible guess at its cause in terms of the training samples.

lab.submit: Paste your completed test_log.txt: your classes and their sample counts, your tests with predictions and confidence, how many were right, the accuracy per class from Under the hood, and your biggest surprise.

modules.title: AI in daily life and at work
modules.summary: See where AI already works in everyday products and workplaces, how chat assistants produce their answers, and how to put one to work on a real task while checking what it gives you.

lessons.title: The AI you already use
objectives: Recognise everyday products that use machine learning
Describe, for one product, what it learned from, what it predicts and what happens when it's wrong
key_points: Email spam filters learn from messages that people mark as spam, and predict for each new message whether it's junk.
Recommendation systems on video, music and shopping sites predict what you're likely to watch, play or buy next, from your history and from people with similar habits.
Phones use machine learning for face unlock, searching photos by what's in them, predictive text and voice typing.
Maps apps predict journey times from live and past traffic data, and banks score card payments for signs of fraud as they happen.
Three questions open up any AI product: what data did it learn from, what does it predict, and what happens when it's wrong?

lessons.title: Generative AI and chat assistants
objectives: Explain how a large language model produces text
Write a clear request (a prompt) and improve the answer with follow-up messages
key_points: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on a vast amount of text to predict the next small piece of text, called a token; chat assistants such as Claude are built on LLMs.
After that first training, models are trained further, including with human feedback, to follow instructions and to be more helpful and less harmful.
An LLM writes text that is likely given what it learned, not text it has checked, so it can state false things fluently and confidently; this is often called hallucination.
A good prompt says what you want, who it's for, the context the assistant needs and the format of the answer; follow-up messages refine it, because the assistant sees the whole conversation.
A model's knowledge stops at the date its training data was collected, so it may not know about recent events unless the assistant can search the web or you give it the information.

steps.do: Open a chat assistant, such as Claude at claude.ai, and start a new chat.
Ask a vague question and look at what comes back.
steps.see: A long, general answer that might suit anyone, so it doesn't quite suit you.

steps.do: Ask again, this time with your situation, the audience and the format you want.
steps.code: I run a small bakery with four staff. In five bullet points, explain to my staff what a chat assistant could help us with day to day, and one thing we shouldn't trust it with.

steps.do: Refine the answer with a follow-up message instead of starting again.
steps.code: Make it shorter, and give a one-line example for each point.

steps.do: Ask it where it's least certain.
steps.code: Which of these points are you least sure about, and how could I check them?

steps.do: Check one factual claim from the answer yourself, against a source you trust. Treat the answer as a draft until you have.

lessons.title: AI at work: tasks, not whole jobs
objectives: Break a job into tasks and judge which ones AI could help with
Plan how a person stays in charge of work that AI helps with
key_points: AI changes work task by task: most jobs mix tasks it can help with, such as drafting, summarising and sorting, with tasks that need human judgement, relationships and responsibility.

Good first uses are tasks where a draft saves time and a person can easily check the result: first drafts of emails, summaries of long documents, ideas for a plan, or explanations of unfamiliar terms.
Keep a person in the loop for decisions that affect people, such as hiring, lending, health or legal matters; whoever uses AI stays responsible for what it produces.
Before using an AI tool at work, check your organisation's policy: which tools are approved, what data you may share, and whether you must say when AI helped.
Find out whether it really helps by trying the same task with and without AI and comparing the time taken and the quality, instead of assuming it saves time.

walkthrough.title: Break a job into tasks with a chat assistant

steps.do: Describe a role, without confidential details, and ask for its everyday tasks.
steps.code: I work as a receptionist at a dental clinic. List the tasks in a typical week, grouped by type.

steps.do: Ask which tasks an assistant could help with, and how a person would check each result.
steps.code: For each task, say whether a chat assistant could help, how, and what a person would need to check before using the result.

steps.do: Push back where the list doesn't match reality: it knows jobs in general, not your workplace.
steps.code: We don't handle billing at the front desk. Remove that, and add confirming appointments by text message.

steps.do: Choose one low-risk task, such as drafting a reminder message, and try it with made-up details rather than real patients' information.

lab.title: Put a chat assistant to work, and check its answers
lab.goal: Use a chat assistant on a realistic work task, turning a long notice into a summary, answers and a reply to a customer, and check every fact it gives against the source, so you see both how much it helps and where it goes wrong.
setup: A free account with a chat assistant such as Claude
Download bus_notice.txt, a made-up notice from a made-up bus company

steps.do: Read bus_notice.txt yourself first, and note how long it takes.
Start a new chat, paste in the whole notice, and ask for a summary for passengers.
steps.code:
Here is a notice from a bus company. Summarise it in five bullet points for passengers, in plain English.

[paste the notice here]

steps.do: Check the summary line by line against the notice. Mark each fact Correct, Wrong, or Not in the notice (something the assistant added).
In the same chat, ask three questions, one at a time.
steps.code:
1. When does the Market Street stop reopen?
2. Does Route 7 run on public holidays?
3. How much will a weekly pass cost a student after the change?

steps.do: Work out the answers yourself from the notice. The notice says nothing about public holidays, so a good answer says the notice doesn't say. For the student pass, take 25% off the new weekly price.
Ask for a reply to a customer, then check its facts the same way.
steps.code: Write a short, polite reply to a passenger who complains that her stop on Market Street has disappeared.

steps.do: Finish with two lines of reflection: Time saved: how long the assistant's version took compared with doing it yourself. Must check: what a person must always check before sending something like this.

checks.text: The summary is pasted, and every fact in it is marked Correct, Wrong or Not in the notice.
The reopening date is checked against the notice: the Market Street stop reopens on Saturday 5 April.
The public holiday answer is judged correctly: the notice doesn't say, so the assistant should say so rather than guess.
The student weekly pass is worked out and checked: 25% off 14.00 is 10.50.
The reply to the customer is checked for facts, such as the temporary stop on Mill Lane.
The reflection says what time was saved and what a person must always check.

lab.submit: Paste the assistant's summary with each fact marked, its three answers with your verdict on each, its reply to the customer with your fact check, and your Time saved and Must check lines.

files.content:
A FICTIONAL NOTICE, MADE UP FOR THIS LAB
----------------------------------------

ASHBY VALE BUSES: CHANGES TO ROUTE 7 AND FARES

From Monday 3 March, Route 7 (Station Square to Hillside Park) will run every 20 minutes
between 07:00 and 19:00, Monday to Saturday. In the evening it will run every 30 minutes,
with the last bus leaving Station Square at 23:00. The Sunday timetable does not change:
a bus every hour from 09:00 to 18:00.

Roadworks: the Market Street stop will be closed from Monday 10 March until Friday 4 April,
and will reopen on Saturday 5 April. While it is closed, please use the temporary stop on
Mill Lane, about 150 metres away, outside the library.

Fares: from 3 March a single ticket will cost 2.20, up from 2.00. A weekly pass will cost
14.00, up from 12.00. Children under 5 travel free with a paying adult. Students who show a
valid student card get 25% off weekly passes. Single tickets for students do not change.

New buses: six new low-floor buses will join Route 7 in March. Each has space for two
wheelchairs or pushchairs and shows the next stop on a screen and by announcement.

Questions: call the travel line on 0100 555 0170 (08:00 to 18:00, Monday to Friday), or ask
the driver.

hints: Not in the notice is for anything the assistant added that the notice doesn't say, even if it sounds sensible.
If the assistant guesses about public holidays, ask it: Where in the notice does it say that? and see what it does.

modules.title: Limits and risks
modules.summary: Learn why AI systems get things wrong, how bias gets into them and how to protect privacy and stay safe, then stress-test your own model to find where it fails and fix it with better data.

lessons.title: Why AI gets things wrong
objectives: Explain why models fail on data unlike the data they learned from
Recognise shortcuts, overconfidence and made-up facts as common ways AI fails
key_points: A model works best on data like its training examples; when what it meets is different, such as new lighting, cameras, accents or customers, its accuracy can drop sharply.
Models can learn shortcuts: patterns that happened to go with the right answer in the training data, such as a background or a watermark, instead of the thing that matters.
A high confidence score isn't proof: a classifier can give a confident answer for an input unlike anything it was trained on.
Language models can invent facts, quotes and references that sound right, so checking against reliable sources is part of using them.
Most models learn which things tend to go together in the data, not what causes what, so they can't say why something happens or what would change if you acted differently.

steps.do: Ask about something that doesn't exist, phrased as if it does.
steps.code: Summarise the main findings of the 2019 Ashby Vale Buses passenger survey.
steps.see: Ashby Vale is made up. A good answer says it can't find or doesn't know of such a survey; an invented summary is a hallucination.

steps.do: Ask for sources for a real topic, then try to open and read each one.
steps.code: Give me three sources, with links, about how spam filters use machine learning.

steps.do: Ask about something recent and see whether it mentions that its knowledge stops at a certain date, or searches the web if it can.
Note which answers sounded confident but couldn't be checked. Those are the ones to treat with the most care.

lessons.title: Bias and fairness
objectives: Explain how bias in data and design leads to unfair results
Suggest checks that show whether a system works equally well for different groups
key_points: Bias in AI usually comes from data: if some groups are missing, under-represented or unfairly described in the examples, the model learns that imbalance.
In 2018 the Gender Shades study found that commercial face-analysis systems were far less accurate at classifying the gender of darker-skinned women than of lighter-skinned men.
Historical data repeats historical decisions: in 2018 Reuters reported that Amazon had scrapped an experimental hiring tool that had learned to mark down CVs containing the word "women's".
Leaving out a characteristic such as sex or ethnicity doesn't remove bias, because other data, such as a postcode or a hobby, can stand in for it.
Checking fairness means measuring how well a system works for each group separately, not only overall: a good overall score can hide poor results for some people.
Remedies include more representative data, testing with the people affected, and a person who can review and overturn the system's decisions.

lessons.title: Privacy, security and using AI responsibly
objectives: Decide what information is safe to share with an AI tool
Recognise deepfakes and over-trust, and the habits that protect against them
key_points: What you type or upload into an online AI service is sent to its provider; depending on the service and your settings it may be stored, reviewed or used to improve models, so read its privacy terms and settings.
Tools differ: Teachable Machine trains in your browser, and your samples aren't sent to any server unless you save the project to Google Drive.
Don't paste personal, confidential or customer information into a tool your organisation hasn't approved; remove names and details, or use made-up examples.

Generative AI can make realistic fake images, voices and videos, called deepfakes; be wary of surprising media, check where it came from, and confirm urgent requests, such as a call asking for money, another way.
People tend to trust automated systems too much, which is called automation bias; deciding in advance what you will check keeps you in charge.

lab.title: Find where your model fails
lab.goal: Stress-test the classifier from module 1 to find where it fails, explain each failure in terms of its training data, then improve the data and run the same tests again.
setup: Your Teachable Machine project from module 1 (or a new one made the same way)
The same three objects, plus a few things that belong to none of your classes

steps.do: Open your project from the menu at the top left: Open project from Drive, or Open project from file. Click Train Model so Preview works again.
Run every test in stress_test.txt before changing anything: lighting, background, distance and angle, look-alikes, and None of these. Record each prediction and its confidence in the Before column.

Look closely at the None of these tests. Whatever you show it, the model still picks one of your classes, often with high confidence. Write down why: it can only choose among the classes it was trained on.
For the two worst failures, write Failure and Why: what went wrong, and what about the training samples explains it (for example, every sample had the same background).
Improve the data. Add samples of each object in the conditions it failed in, then click Add a class, name it Nothing, and record the empty background and some random objects. Click Train Model again.
Run exactly the same tests again and fill in the After column.
steps.see: Fewer mistakes in the conditions you added samples for, and None of these inputs now going to Nothing.

steps.do: Count the right answers before and after, and open Advanced, Under the hood, to compare the accuracy per class.

checks.text: At least twelve tests across at least four conditions are recorded before any changes, with each prediction and its confidence.
Inputs that belong to no class were tested, and the write-up explains that the model can only choose among its own classes.
Each main failure is explained in terms of the training data, such as backgrounds or lighting the samples didn't cover.
The model was improved by changing the data, including a Nothing class, and retested on the same tests.
The number right before and after is compared.

lab.submit: Paste your completed stress_test.txt: every test with its before and after predictions, the scores before and after, your two main failures with why, what you changed, and what the None of these tests show.

Change one thing at a time where you can, so you know which change helped.
If your project didn't save, make a new one with the same objects first; it takes about ten minutes.

modules.title: Reading AI news critically
modules.summary: Learn the questions that cut through hype, what accuracy figures really mean and how to check sources and AI-made content, then put an AI press release under the microscope.

lessons.title: Hype, headlines and what's really new
objectives: Ask the key questions about any AI claim: what task, what data, compared with what, and who says so
Recognise common signs of hype in AI coverage
key_points: Start with the task: what exactly did the system do, on what kind of data and in what setting? A headline such as 'AI beats doctors' may describe one narrow test.
Ask 'compared with what?': a result means little without a baseline, such as how well people, older methods or a simple rule do on the same test.
Check the source: a peer-reviewed paper, an independent evaluation, a company press release and a social media demo are very different kinds of evidence.
A demo may be the best of many tries; ask whether the system works reliably on everyday inputs, not just on chosen examples.
Watch for words that give machines human qualities, such as 'understands', 'thinks' or 'wants', and for 'AI' used as a label for ordinary software.

walkthrough.title: Use a chat assistant as a critical-reading partner

steps.do: Find a recent news article about an AI system and copy its text, or a long extract.
Ask the assistant to separate the claims from the evidence.
steps.code:
List each claim this article makes about the AI system and, for each one, the evidence the article gives for it. Quote the article's words.

[paste the article here]

steps.do: Ask for the questions a sceptical reader should ask.
steps.code: What questions would a sceptical science reporter ask about these claims? Which of them does the article leave unanswered?

steps.do: Check the list against the article yourself: an assistant can misread, leave things out or add things. Keep what holds up.

lessons.title: Making sense of accuracy claims
objectives: Explain why accuracy depends on the test data and on how common the thing being detected is
Work out what a detection rate means for a realistic group of people
key_points: Accuracy is measured on a particular test set; a model tested on clean, carefully chosen data usually does worse on messy real-world data.
For rare events accuracy can mislead: if 1 payment in 1,000 is fraud, a detector that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate and catches nothing.
Two numbers say more than accuracy alone: how many of the real cases the system catches, and how many false alarms it raises.

Worked example: if 1 person in 1,000 has a condition, and a test catches 99% of cases but wrongly flags 1% of healthy people, then among 100,000 people it flags 99 real cases and 999 healthy people, so most of its alarms are false.
Ask who was in the test: a result from one hospital, one country or one age group may not hold for other people.

lessons.title: Checking sources and AI-made content
objectives: Check a claim or an image by finding out what other sources say about it
Explain why spotting AI-made content by eye or with detectors is unreliable
key_points: Lateral reading means leaving the page to see what independent sources say about a claim and about whoever made it, instead of judging a page by how professional it looks.
A reverse image search shows where else a picture has appeared, which can reveal an old photo reused or an image taken out of context.
AI-made images, voices and text are getting harder to spot by eye, and tools that claim to detect AI-written text are unreliable, so check the source rather than relying on a feeling or a detector.
Some cameras, apps and publishers attach provenance information, such as Content Credentials, that records how an image was made or edited, but most content online doesn't carry it.
Before you share something surprising, check who first published it, when, and whether trusted outlets report the same thing.

lab.title: Put an AI press release under the microscope
lab.goal: Read a made-up company's press release about a skin-cancer app, work out what its numbers really show, find what's missing, and write a short, fair verdict.
setup: Download press_release.txt, a press release invented for this lab
A chat assistant such as Claude (optional: the lab can be done without one)

steps.do: Read press_release.txt and underline every claim: in the headline, in the quote and in the body.
Work out what the 98% means: how many photos it got right out of how many, and how many of the 400 photos showed melanoma at all.
Work out what matters most for a cancer check: of the 20 melanomas, how many did it catch, as a percentage? How many harmless moles did it wrongly flag?
Look at the comparison with dermatologists. Were they tested on the same photos, at the same time, in the same way?
Look at who and what was tested: where the photos came from, how they were taken, and who the patients were. Compare that with how the app will be used.
Optionally, paste the press release into a chat assistant and ask what a sceptical reader would question. Check its answer against the text: did it catch the 15 out of 20?
Write your analysis under six headings: Task:, Evidence:, Compared with:, Who was tested:, Missing:, and Verdict: (two or three fair sentences).

checks.text: The 98% is explained: 392 of 400 photos were right, but most photos weren't melanoma, so accuracy alone flatters the app.
The share of melanomas caught is worked out: 15 of 20, which is 75%, so it missed 5 in 20.
The comparison with dermatologists is questioned, because they weren't tested on the same photos.
Who was tested is questioned: one clinic, professional photos, mostly older patients with fair skin, while the app is for anyone's phone photos.
What's missing is listed, such as independent review or published results, and the verdict is fair and follows from the evidence.

lab.submit: Paste your analysis under the six headings (Task, Evidence, Compared with, Who was tested, Missing, Verdict), with your working for the 98% and for the share of melanomas caught.

files.content:
A FICTIONAL PRESS RELEASE, MADE UP FOR THIS LAB
-----------------------------------------------
Kestrel Diagnostics and SkinCheck are invented names. Any resemblance to a real company or
product is accidental.

KESTREL DIAGNOSTICS LAUNCHES SKINCHECK AI:
"SPOTS SKIN CANCER WITH 98% ACCURACY, OUTPERFORMING DERMATOLOGISTS"

Kestrel Diagnostics today announced SkinCheck AI, a phone app that tells users whether a
mole could be melanoma, a dangerous skin cancer, from a single photo.

"SkinCheck thinks like a dermatologist, only faster," said Kestrel's chief executive. "Soon
nobody will need to wait for a skin check again."

In Kestrel's own study, SkinCheck was tested on 400 photos of moles from its partner clinic.
It classified 392 of the 400 photos correctly: an accuracy of 98%. A survey published in
another country several years ago found that dermatologists' accuracy was around 90%.

Study details: the 400 photos were taken by clinic staff with a professional camera under
the clinic's lights. 20 of the photos showed melanoma and 380 did not. SkinCheck flagged 15
of the 20 melanomas, and wrongly flagged 3 of the 380 harmless moles. Most patients at the
clinic were over 50 and had fair skin. The study has not been published or independently
reviewed.

SkinCheck AI will be available for phones next month for a monthly subscription.

Small print: SkinCheck AI is not a medical device and does not give a diagnosis. Always
consult a doctor about changes to your skin.

hints: 380 of the 400 photos weren't melanoma, so an app that never flagged anything would still be right 380 times out of 400: 95%.
The small print and the headline make different promises: compare them.

project.title: An AI decision brief
project.brief: Choose an AI tool that is used, or being considered, in your workplace, school or community: for example a chat assistant for customer emails, a CV-screening service, a crop-disease app or a camera that counts visitors. Write a brief of about two pages, in plain language and without code, for the person who has to decide whether to use it. Explain what the tool does and what it learned from; try it, or a similar free tool, and record your tests, including ones designed to find where it fails; weigh its benefits against risks such as errors, bias and privacy; list the questions you would put to its maker; and end with a recommendation and the conditions that should come with it. You may use a chat assistant, but check everything it tells you and say where you used it.
deliverables: A plain-language explanation of the tool: what it predicts or produces, and what data it learned from (or most likely learned from)
A test log of at least ten tries of the tool, or a similar free one, including at least three designed to find where it fails
A table of benefits and risks, covering errors, bias, privacy and security, and who could be harmed
Five questions for the tool's maker or seller, each with a sentence on why it matters
A recommendation (use, trial with conditions, or don't use) that says how a person stays in charge
A short note on where you used a chat assistant and how you checked what it said

rubric.name: Clear, accurate explanation
rubric.description: Explains what the tool does and how it learned in plain language, using the course's ideas (training data, model, prediction, confidence) correctly.

rubric.name: Testing
rubric.description: At least ten recorded tests, including at least three aimed at failures; results are reported honestly, with what they suggest about the tool.

rubric.name: Risks and fairness
rubric.description: Names specific risks rather than generic ones, says who could be harmed, and considers how errors, bias and privacy problems could arise.

rubric.name: Questions and evidence
rubric.description: Sharp questions about data, testing and baselines; claims are checked against sources, and no statistic appears without one.

rubric.name: Recommendation
rubric.description: A clear recommendation that follows from the evidence, with conditions and a person who can review the tool's decisions.

rubric.name: Transparency
rubric.description: Says where a chat assistant helped and how its output was checked.

project.submit: Paste your brief: the explanation, the test log, the benefits and risks table, your five questions and your recommendation, followed by your note on where you used a chat assistant. Links to the sources you checked are welcome.
